definitions.definition: In BhG 7–9: the knowledge of the Lord 'entire' (samagra) that Kṛṣṇa declares together with vijñāna; having known it nothing further remains to be known (7.2), and one is freed from the inauspicious (9.1). Its bearer, the jñānin, is foremost of the four kinds of devotees (7.16–18).

Paired with jñāna as its complement in the knowledge Kṛṣṇa declares 'with vijñāna' (jñānaṃ savijñānam, 7.2; jñānaṃ vijñānasahitam, 9.1). The text does not define the difference; commentators take it as realization of what is taught, or as knowledge of the Lord's distinguishing particulars.

The Lord's lower nature, divided eightfold: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind (manas), intellect (buddhi) and I-maker (ahaṃkāra) (7.4–5); with the higher nature it is the source of all beings (7.6).
The Lord's other, higher nature, 'which has become the living being' (jīvabhūtā) and by which the world is upheld (7.5); together with the lower it is the womb of all beings (7.6).

In BhG 7–9: (a) the Lord's own nature, lower (eightfold) and higher (7.4–6); at the close of a kalpa beings go into it and, taking hold of it, he sends them forth again, helpless under its power (9.7–8); with him as overseer it gives birth to the moving and unmoving (9.10); (b) a person's own nature, which constrains the worship chosen (7.20); (c) the divine nature (daivī) resorted to by the great-souled, and the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras resorted to by the deluded (9.12–13).

The Lord's divine (daivī) māyā, made of the guṇas and hard to get beyond; those who take refuge in him alone cross it (7.14). It carries off the knowledge of evil-doers, who do not take refuge in him (7.15).
That by which the Lord is veiled, so that he is not manifest to all; through it the deluded world does not recognize him, the unborn and imperishable (7.25).

Expressed in BhG 7–9 by forms of pra-√pad and vy-apa-√śri: those who take refuge in the Lord alone cross his māyā (7.14); evil-doers do not (7.15); at the end of many births the knower takes refuge knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' (7.19); people driven by desires take refuge in other deities (7.20); by taking refuge in him even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras reach the highest goal (9.32).

The states (bhāva) of sattva, rajas and tamas come from the Lord, yet he is not in them (7.12); deluded by these three guṇa-made states the world does not recognize him, who is beyond them (7.13); his māyā is 'made of the guṇas' (7.14).
The Lord declares himself the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8).
'Oṃ, the one-syllabled Brahman' (om ity ekākṣaraṃ brahma), to be uttered, while remembering the Lord, by one who departs abandoning the body; he goes to the supreme goal (8.13).
Among the Lord's self-identifications: 'the oṃkāra, and the Ṛk, the Sāman and the Yajus' (9.17).

Brahman is the supreme imperishable (8.3); the imperishable that knowers of the Veda declare, which passionless ascetics enter and for which people practise brahmacarya (8.11); the unmanifest beyond the cosmic unmanifest is called the imperishable, the supreme goal from which there is no return, the Lord's supreme abode (8.20–21). Oṃ is the 'one-syllabled' (ekākṣara) Brahman (8.13).

In BhG 7–9: asked about by Arjuna (8.1) and defined as 'the supreme imperishable' (akṣaraṃ paramam, 8.3); known by those who, taking refuge in the Lord, strive for release from old age and death (7.29); knowers of Brahman go to Brahman on the bright course (8.24); Oṃ is the one-syllabled Brahman (8.13).
Defined as (Brahman's) own being (svabhāva) (8.3); known 'in its entirety' by those who strive for release taking refuge in the Lord (7.29).
In 8.3 the definition of adhyātma: 'own being' (svabhāvo 'dhyātmam ucyate), following the definition of Brahman as the supreme imperishable.

notes: Whose 'own being' is meant (Brahman's, as the inner self, or the individual's) is decided by commentators, not by the verse.

definitions.definition: In 8.3 the definition of karma: 'the visarga that brings about the coming-into-being of beings' existence' (bhūta-bhāvodbhava-karo visargaḥ karma-saṃjñitaḥ).

notes: Commentators read it as the sacrificial release of oblations that sustains the arising of beings, or as creative emission.

definitions.definition: In BhG 7–9: defined as the emission (visarga) that brings beings into existence (8.3); known in its entirety by those striving for release (7.29); the Lord's creative acts do not bind him, seated as if indifferent (9.9); acts done as an offering to him free one from the bonds of action with their good and bad fruits (9.27–28).
The perishable state (kṣaro bhāvaḥ) (8.4); to be known together with the Lord (7.30), asked about at 8.1.
Named with adhibhūta and adhiyajña as what one should know with the Lord (7.30); asked about at 8.1 and answered (as adhidaivata) at 8.4: it is the Person (puruṣa).
In 8.4: 'the adhidaivata is the Person (puruṣa)' — the answer to Arjuna's question about the adhidaiva (8.1).
The Lord himself, 'here in the body' (8.4); Arjuna asked who it is and how it is present in the body (8.2).
'The perishable state' (kṣaro bhāvaḥ) is the adhibhūta (8.4); contrasted with Brahman the supreme imperishable (8.3).

The time of death, also called prayāṇa-kāla, 'time of departure': those with minds yoked know the Lord even then (7.30; asked at 8.2); whoever departs remembering him then comes to his state (8.5); one goes to whatever state one remembers at the end, as habitually dwelt on (8.6); at that time the yogin sets the breath between the brows (8.10).

Remembrance of the Lord (verbs smṛ, anu-smṛ, anu-cint): at the end, which determines one's destination (8.5–6); at all times, while fighting (8.7); constantly, with the mind on nothing else, which makes him easy to reach (8.14); as meditation on the ancient seer beyond darkness (8.8–9); joined with uttering Oṃ at departure (8.13).
In 8.8: with a mind yoked by the yoga of repeated practice, not straying to anything else, one who meditates constantly goes to the supreme divine Person.
In 8.10: at departure the yogin, yoked with devotion and 'by the power of yoga', makes the breath enter fully between the brows.
'Established in yoga-dhāraṇā' (8.12): the holding with which the departing yogin restrains the gates, confines the mind in the heart and places the breath in the head.

Used in three connected ways in BhG 7–9: (a) the Lord as unmanifest, whom the unintelligent think to have come into manifestation (7.24), whose unmanifest form pervades all this (9.4); (b) the cosmic unmanifest from which manifest things come forth at the coming of Brahmā's day and into which they dissolve at night (8.18); (c) another, eternal unmanifest beyond that one, which does not perish when beings perish, called the imperishable, the supreme goal, the Lord's supreme abode (8.20–21).
Manifest things (vyaktayaḥ) that come forth from the unmanifest at the coming of day (8.18); the unintelligent think the Lord, the unmanifest, has come into manifestation (vyakti) (7.24).
Brahmā's day lasts a thousand yugas and his night ends after a thousand yugas; those who know this 'know day and night' (8.17).
At the close of a kalpa (kalpa-kṣaya) all beings go into the Lord's prakṛti; at the beginning of a kalpa he sends them forth again (9.7).
The Lord is the origin and the dissolution of the whole world (7.6; 9.18); manifest things dissolve (pra-√lī) into the unmanifest at the coming of Brahmā's night (8.18–19).

The Gītā does not use the word; it speaks of the 'bright course' (śukla gati): fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course — departing there, knowers of Brahman go to Brahman (8.24); by it one goes to non-return (8.26).

The Gītā does not use the word; it speaks of the 'dark course' (kṛṣṇa gati): smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the southern course — there the yogin reaches the lunar light and returns (8.25–26).
The six months of the northern course, the last-named station of the bright course by which knowers of Brahman go to Brahman (8.24).
The six months of the southern course, the last-named station of the dark course, on which the yogin reaches the lunar light and returns (8.25).

Expressed in BhG 8 as anāvṛtti and 'no rebirth': having come to the Lord the great-souled do not come to rebirth, the impermanent abode of sorrow (8.15–16), whereas all worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return; reaching the imperishable they do not return (8.21); the bright course leads to non-return, the dark to return (8.23, 8.26).
'My supreme abode' — the unmanifest imperishable, the supreme goal, reaching which they do not return (8.21).
The knowledge Kṛṣṇa declares in ch. 9: royal knowledge, royal secret, the supreme purifier, known by direct apprehension, in accord with dharma, very easy to practise, imperishable (9.2).
The teaching of ch. 9 is 'most secret' (guhyatama), to be told to one free of cavilling (9.1), and 'the royal secret' (rājaguhya) (9.2).
In 9.15: others worship the Lord by sacrificing with the sacrifice of knowledge — as one, as distinct, in many ways, him who faces in all directions.
What the Lord himself carries (vahāmi) for those who, with nothing else, think of him and worship him, ever devoted (9.22).

Expressed in BhG 8–9 as ananya-cetas (8.14), bhaktyā ananyayā (8.22), ananya-manas (9.13), ananyāḥ (9.22) and ananya-bhāk (9.30): by it the supreme Person is gained (8.22); for the one who remembers him so he is easy to reach (8.14); he carries the welfare of such devotees (9.22); even one of very bad conduct who worships so is to be considered good (9.30).

In BhG 7–9: four kinds of people of good deeds worship (bhaj) the Lord, the knower of single devotion (eka-bhakti) being foremost (7.16–17); devotion joins yoga-power at departure (8.10); the supreme Person is gained by undivided devotion (8.22); the great-souled bow to him with devotion (9.14); he partakes of a leaf, flower, fruit or water offered with devotion (9.26); those who worship him with devotion are in him and he in them (9.29); his devotee does not perish (9.31); be my devotee (9.34).
The Lord, sending forth the beings, is 'seated as one indifferent' (udāsīnavat), unattached to those acts, and so they do not bind him (9.9).
With the Lord as overseer (adhyakṣa), prakṛti gives birth to the moving and the unmoving, and so the world revolves (9.10).
Among the Lord's self-identifications: goal, upholder, lord, witness (sākṣin), dwelling, refuge, friend (9.18).
The knowers of the three Vedas (traividyāḥ), soma-drinkers, win heaven by sacrifice (9.20); following the dharma of the three (trayī-dharma), desiring desires, they obtain going and coming (9.21).

The way to heaven (svargati) prayed for by Vedic sacrificers; they reach the world of the lord of the gods and enjoy divine enjoyments, and when their merit is spent they enter the mortal world again (9.20–21).

Mind and intellect offered to the Lord (mayy arpita-mano-buddhiḥ, 8.7); whatever one does, eats, sacrifices, gives or practises as austerity is to be done 'as an offering to me' (mad-arpaṇa, 9.27), which frees from the bonds of action (9.28).
In 9.28 'saṃnyāsa-yoga': the self yoked in the yoga of renunciation — here the offering of all acts to the Lord of 9.27 — frees one from the bonds of action so that one comes to him.

The rare one who at the end of many births takes refuge knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' (7.19); those who have reached the highest perfection and are not reborn (8.15); those of divine nature who worship the Lord with undivided mind (9.13).
The fourth of the four kinds of devotees; ever yoked, of single devotion, he is foremost; the Lord is exceedingly dear to him and he to the Lord; the Lord holds him to be his very self (7.16–18).
Kṛṣṇa's name for himself in 7.19: the rare great soul takes refuge in him knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' (vāsudevaḥ sarvam).

notes: The Gītā verse gives no etymology of the name.

definitions.definition: Whatever form a devotee wishes to worship with faith, the Lord makes that faith unwavering, and through it the devotee obtains desires ordained by the Lord (7.21–22); those without faith in this dharma return to saṃsāra (9.3); devotees of other deities who sacrifice with faith sacrifice to him, not by the rule (9.23).

The 'delusion of the pairs' (dvandva-moha), arising from desire and aversion, into which all beings fall at birth (7.27); those whose sin has ended are freed from it and worship the Lord firm in vows (7.28).
The Lord is the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices; not recognizing him in truth, worshippers of other deities fall (9.24).

The 'demonic state' (āsura bhāva) resorted to by evil-doers whose knowledge is carried off by māyā, who do not take refuge in the Lord (7.15); the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras resorted to by those who disregard him (9.12).
The great-souled always glorify the Lord (kīrtayantaḥ), strive, keep firm vows and bow to him with devotion (9.14).
Bowing to the Lord with devotion (namasyantaḥ, 9.14); 'bow to me' (māṃ namaskuru) in the closing injunction (9.34).

In BhG 8: the adhidaivata is 'the Person' (8.4); constant meditation leads to 'the supreme divine Person' (paramaṃ puruṣaṃ divyam) (8.8, 8.10); that supreme Person, in whom beings abide and by whom all is pervaded, is gained by undivided devotion (8.22).
The form (of a deity) which a devotee wishes to worship with faith (7.21); the human body (mānuṣī tanu) the Lord has taken, for which the deluded disregard him (9.11).

Among thousands hardly one strives for perfection, and of the striving/perfected hardly one knows the Lord in truth (7.3); the great-souled reach the highest perfection (saṃsiddhi) and are not reborn (8.15).
